caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 788 Of 2000.
lawyer: For the Petitioner: Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, Senior Advocate (Kazi Shahabuddin Ahmed, Advocate with him), instructed by Mr. Md. Nawab Ali, Advocate-on-Record. Respondent: Not represented.
parties:
Abdul Latif Milki ------ Petitioner.
Versus
Syed Mamun Murshed ------ Respondent
full_judgment:
Mr. Mainur Reza Chowdhury, J: The petitioner seeks leave to appeal against the judgment and order passed by Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1015 of 1990 making the rule absolute setting aside the judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 55 of 1989 and reversing those of the learned Additional Assistant Judge, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 41 of 1988 decreeing the plaintiff's suit for permanent injunction. 

 2. The facts in short are that the respondent Syed Mamun Mushed instituted the above title suit for permanent injunction. His case that the suit shop being No. B/2, South Gulshan Market was allotted to one Badruddin Chowdhury who had no capital to start a business in the said shop and accordingly approached one Christopher C. Gomez to invest capital in order to start a business in the said premises. Christopher C. Gomez agreed to the proposal and entered into the partnership business by executing a deed of partnership dated 01.07.1978 and started business in tilt me and style "G.C. Traders". The said Christopher C. Gomez invested the capital in business of Electronic goods and accessories. Subsequently Badruddin Chowdhury decided to retire from the partnership business and he transferred his interest in the business and possession in the suit shop for valuable consideration to Christopher C. Gomez who being the owner in possession sold the shop room to the plaintiff respondent on 06.05.1980 and since then the respondent being in possession of the suit shop. 

 4. The learned Assistant Judge on consideration of the evidence on record found the plaintiff respondent is in possession of the suit promises, He also found that the defendant's case was not believable and therefore decreed the suit. 

 5. On appeal the learned Subordinate Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka held that the since complicated question in title is involved in the suit and accordingly the suit for permanent injunction was not maintainable. The possession of the plaintiff respondent in the suit shop premises was that of trespasser. It was found that the suit was bad for defect of parties and accordingly by the judgment and decree allowed the appeal reversing the decision of the trial court and dismissed the plaintiff's suit. 

 6. In civil revision it was submitted by the learned Counsel for the plaintiff respondent that the learned Subordinate Judge committed a gross error of law in holding that a suit for permanent injunction was not maintainable as a complicated question of title is involved overlooking that the plaintiff had proved his prima facie title and exclusive possession in the suit shop premises and that in a suit for permanent injunction investigation as to the title is not legally required though the question of title may be incidentally gone in a suit for permanent injunction. The lower appellate court having found that the plaintiff respondent has been in possession of the suit shop as a trespasser should have decreed the suit inasmuch as even a trespasser is entitled to maintain his possession against the whole world except the real owner until evicted in due process of law. It was further argued that the learned Subordinate Judge had committed a gross illegality in holding that the suit was bad for defect of parties overlooking that in a suit for permanent injunction, relief may be claimed only against the persons who threatens the possession of the plaintiff and persons who do not threaten the possession of the plaintiff are not necessary parties to be impleaded in the suit for permanent injunction. On the other hand it was submitted by the learned counsel for the defendant petitioner that in a suit for permanent injunction the plaintiff must prove that he has legal possession in the suit shop to transfer of the suit shop made by Christopher C. Gomez in favour of the plaintiff respondent on 06.05.1980 which is not permissible under section 19 of the partnership Act. In the absence of any evidence of retirement of the partner namely, Chowdhury Badruddin, Christopher C. Gomez could not along make any transfer in favour of the plaintiff respondent. Accordingly the plaintiff respondent had no prima facie title in the suit premises and therefore, the suit for permanent injunction was not maintainable. 

 7. The trial court carefully considered the submissions made by the learned counsel for the respective parties. It was found that the plaintiff claims that there was a clause in the partnership deed that in the event Chowdhury Badruddin retires from business, he would transfer the suit shop in favour of Christopher C. Gomez and accordingly the plaintiff respondent had been in possession of the suit shop premises by purchase from Christopher C. Gomez taking one Nahal Uddin as a partner with him. The trial Court considered the evidence of P.W. 1-6 and found that the plaintiff had been in possession of the suit shop premises and it is stated in para- 13 of the written statement wherein the defendant admit that the plaintiff respondent in collusion with Christopher C. Gomez entered into the suit promises by forte and attempted to mutate his name. From the statement in para-13 of the written statement the trial court found that the plaintiff respondent was admittedly in possession of the suit shop premises. The trial court also found from evidence that the possession of the suit shop was not transferred to the defendant. The lower appellate court found that the defendant petitioner clearly claimed that the document dated 20.12.1982 by which Badruddin Chowdhury in favour of Christopher C. Gomez transferred the suit shop was forged, collusive and fraudulent, and the plaintiff respondent did not take any step to prove the said document. Accordingly the lower appellate court found that even if the transfer made by Badruddin Chowdhury in favour of Christopher C. Gomez on 20.12.1982 is accepted, in that case, Christopher C. Gomez could not transfer the suit shop promises to the plaintiff respondent on 06.05.1980 as Christopher C. Gomez had no transferable right on 06.05.1980. Because of this fact the lower appellate court held that the suit involve a complicated question of title and therefore a suit for permanent injunction was not maintainable. 

 8. In the present suit for permanent injunction the plaintiff respondent claims his possessory right on the basis of a document executed by Christopher C. Gomez on 06.05.1980. The defendant petitioner on the other hand claimed his right in possession by purchase from Chowdhury Badruddin on 03.02.1983. The suit is not based on any allegation of threat against the admitted owner Chowdhury Badruddin or from his partner Christopher C. Gomez. It is not disputed that Chowdhury got the suit shop premises by allotment from DIT and Christopher C. Gomez was a partner of Chowdhury Badruddin on the basis of partnership deed on 1.7.1978. Both the courts have concurrently found that the plaintiff respondent has possession in the suit shop premises. The lower appellant court also found that the plaintiff respondent was in possession as a trespasser. The lower appellate court having found that the plaintiff is .in possession of the suit shop as a trespasser but it failed to notice that trespasser is entitled to maintain his possession against all except the real owner who could dispossess him in accordance with law. In the present case, the plaintiff respondent has been seeking protection of his possession against its original owner who is Chowdhury Badruddin. In that view of the matter, both the courts having found that the plaintiff respondent was in possession of the suit shop premises, the instant suit for permanent injunction could not be said to be not maintainable against the defendants petitioner inasmuch as the relief has been sought no against the defendants petitioner inasmuch as the relief has been sought no against the admitted real owner of the suit shop premises. In the case reported in 43 DLR (AD) 215 it has been held that "In a simple suit for permanent injunction with regard to a disputed landed property the relief is available to a  person who is possession. The Court may enquire incidentally late the respective claims of the parties to the suit, for determining whether the plaintiff is in possession of the disputed property and entitled to the specific relief of permanent injunction." The High Court Division therefore made the rule absolute and the impugned judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Dhaka in title Appeal No. 55 of 1989 hereby set aside and those passed by the learned Assistant Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka, in title suit no 41 of 1988 were restored.
